title: The Fall of Kiev
subtitle: German entry into Kiev and the unfinished pocket battle
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: German entry into Kiev began an occupation while the larger encirclement battle continued to the east. Residents confronted damaged services, selective evacuation and new coercive authorities as Soviet soldiers sought routes out.
body:
The army leaves, the city remains

On 19 September 1941, German troops entered Kiev after the Soviet withdrawal. For the military commands, the city’s fall formed part of an encirclement still being fought across a much larger area. For the people who remained, it began a new relationship with armed authority. The departing army could destroy bridges and installations, but it could not take the city’s entire population with it. Residents had to find water and food, locate relatives and interpret unfamiliar orders while soldiers continued fighting east of the Dnieper. Kiev’s fall changed who could issue and enforce orders inside the city while leaving the wider battle unresolved. Its inhabitants now confronted demands whose consequences would reach far beyond the military arrangements for taking possession.[1][2]

The relationship with The Encirclement Closes is essential but brief. German mobile forces had already joined well east of the city. The 37th Army could leave its positions around Kiev without reaching safety, because the route beyond the Dnieper led into the larger pocket. Other Soviet armies were attempting to reorganize or break out farther east. German possession of the city and German destruction of those armies were separate achievements, reached on different schedules. Accounts that end the whole battle on 19 September erase the continuing resistance and the choices still confronting the trapped troops.

Kiev’s inhabitants also entered the day from unequal positions. Some families had left with evacuated institutions, some men had been mobilised, and others remained because they lacked transport, had responsibilities they could not abandon or did not expect occupation to threaten them in the same way. The population visible to the entering Germans was consequently not a representative sample of the prewar city. Evacuation had altered its social composition before the first occupation order appeared. The experiences of those left behind must be understood through that selection as well as through the policies the Germans introduced.

Withdrawal through the Dnieper crossings

The written permission to abandon Kiev was issued at 23.40 on 17 September. It authorized withdrawal to the eastern bank of the Dnieper and required the removal of weapons from the fortified region where possible. Equipment that could not be evacuated was to be destroyed, along with bridges and other military installations. The order ended the demand to retain the city, but its implementation required an army already weakened by prolonged fighting to move through a restricted number of crossings. The same installations that had supported the defence now became bottlenecks through which the defenders had to pass.[3]

The 37th Army’s warning, forwarded to higher command on 17 September, described the immediate danger. German pressure had broken parts of its western defence, while attacks east of the river threatened the crossings from behind. Contact with neighbouring formations was missing, reserves were exhausted and transport was accumulating in Kiev and Darnytsia. These were connected failures. A bridge could remain physically intact while the roads leading away from it became unsafe. Moving another column across would not solve the problem if that column then became trapped in congestion on the eastern bank.[3]

The army was being asked to preserve fighting power while denying useful infrastructure to its pursuers. Those aims could conflict. Guns needed towing vehicles or horses, ammunition required carrying capacity, and wounded men could not necessarily move at the pace of the infantry. Delaying a demolition might allow more Soviet troops to cross but increase the risk that the Germans would seize the bridge. Advancing it might protect the retreating main body while abandoning stragglers. The written order supplied a principle; local commanders still had to judge timing amid incomplete information and changing pressure.

The river’s scale made those decisions especially consequential. Kiev’s western districts stood across a major water barrier from Darnytsia and the roads toward Boryspil and Brovary. A movement out of the city required more than reaching the waterfront. Formations had to preserve enough organisation to use the approaches, cross and then continue toward their assigned destinations. Military transport did not arrive in a single uniform stream. Headquarters vehicles, artillery teams, infantry and supply columns had different speeds and stopping requirements. When those streams mixed under pressure, the obstruction of one could immobilize several others.

The departure took place under the pressure of German infantry armies as well as the distant armoured barrier. The 6th Army under Walter von Reichenau operated against Kiev, and the XXIX Army Corps under Hans von Obstfelder became central to the city’s initial occupation. The capture should therefore not be imagined as the same panzer spearheads simply driving back from their junction to take the city. Mobile formations and infantry were performing related but different tasks: the former had interrupted the Soviet routes east, while the latter pressed and occupied the positions being abandoned.[4][1]

Contemporary accounts from inside Kiev describe destruction and movement without supplying a complete tactical map. Their value lies in showing what the withdrawal meant at street level. An observer could see troops, vehicles or a bridge exploding without knowing whether the movement had been ordered, whether another crossing remained usable or where the army intended to concentrate. Military reports and civilian testimony must therefore be read together. Neither alone gives the full event: headquarters understood intended routes but often lacked the current position of its units, while residents saw the immediate effects without access to the overall plan.

A soldier sheltered on Andriivskyi Descent

In a diary entry dated 25 September, Iryna Khoroshunova recalled a young Soviet soldier running up Andriivskyi Descent as the Germans entered. Women brought him inside, gave him bread and found civilian clothes. Her account describes his distress and his eventual departure that evening, but it does not establish what happened to him afterward. The episode belongs to her recollection of 19 September, written several days later, rather than to a diary entry completed during the encounter. It shows how the distinction between a withdrawing army and a civilian household could suddenly become practical and personal. For the women, helping a soldier meant taking responsibility for someone whom the new authorities might seek. For him, survival briefly depended on people outside his military organisation. The account preserves that encounter without allowing us to invent a later escape or reunion.[5]

The city that could not evacuate itself

Historian Dmytro Malakov’s study of the first occupation days emphasises the selective character of evacuation. Skilled workers and technical staff from important enterprises, officials, prominent cultural figures and their families had opportunities linked to institutional priorities. Their departure emptied particular buildings and neighbourhoods more thoroughly than others. This was not a comprehensive evacuation of the civilian population. The distinction matters because remaining in Kiev cannot be treated as a single political choice. Access to a train, a recognised workplace assignment or a family connection could shape the outcome as decisively as a person’s preference.[6]

Institutional status did not guarantee departure either. Elena Zinkevych and Michelle Assay’s research on the Kiev Conservatoire identifies the absence of an official evacuation for that institution and the consequent presence of many teachers and students during the occupation. This particular finding, stated in the published chapter’s abstract, demonstrates the limits of speaking about a uniformly evacuated cultural elite. Institutions had different resources and administrative histories. A person could possess education and professional standing yet remain without an organised route out. The city left behind contained people whose circumstances cut across simple categories of privilege, loyalty or willingness to flee.[7]

Households also faced decisions that could not be solved through an institutional order. Taking an elderly relative required space, assistance and a destination; leaving that person behind could be unacceptable even when departure was possible for someone younger. Packing possessions consumed time but might preserve the means to survive elsewhere. Information about transport could change faster than a family could act on it. These are not reasons to assume that everyone understood the danger and freely chose to remain. They explain why opportunity, knowledge and responsibility had to coincide before evacuation became a real option.

Food became an immediate concern as the departing authorities ceased normal distribution. Anatolii Pavliuk’s diary for 19 September recorded people carrying flour and even unbaked dough taken from bakeries. The observation is more revealing than a general label of looting. Food in an institution without functioning distribution could be seized for private use, and people needed containers or simply their hands to carry it. Pavliuk’s account does not establish how much food remained in the city or whether every act of taking was driven by hunger. It does show inhabitants trying to turn stocks they could reach into provisions for their households during the collapse of the previous system.[8]

The distinction between food physically present and food available through a dependable system was crucial. A family might acquire something during the transition and still have no means of replacing it. Flour required water, fuel and a place to prepare it. A shop could contain goods while lacking staff, authorization or a secure means of opening. Money retained its physical form even when there was little that could be bought with it. The arrival of a new administration did not automatically restore those relationships. Civilian survival depended on practical exchanges that military possession of the streets did not itself provide.

Protecting the windows with bedding

Nina Herasymova wrote on 18 September that she had covered her windows with a mattress and pillows to protect herself from flying glass. Her diary placed that small household action beside the movement of troops and the loss of water and radio service. On the following day she described the unfamiliar quiet and the appearance of German motorcyclists. The account survives through published selections from her wartime notebooks, rendered in Ukrainian from the original Russian. Its details belong to her position in the city, not to an omniscient account of the withdrawal. The bedding matters because it shows how civilians adapted ordinary possessions to a threat they could not control. Her family could not decide when the army would leave or which installations would be destroyed, but it could attempt to reduce the danger inside its own rooms.[9]

Occupation becomes a system of authority

German occupation began with military institutions already present behind the advancing troops. Berkhoff identifies Alfred von Puttkammer, commander of Rear Army Area 585, as the first city commander, followed on 23 September by Kurt Eberhard of Field Command 175. He also stresses uncertainty about the precise transfer of authority between army and army-group rear commands. The uncertainty does not imply an absence of German authority. It shows overlapping institutions whose responsibilities cannot be reduced to a single official’s title. An advance detachment of Paul Blobel’s Sonderkommando 4a arrived on 19 September, bringing the security-police apparatus into the city from the beginning.[4]

For residents, authority appeared through armed men, notices, requisitions and requirements to register. Malakov records orders appearing on 21 September concerning registration, work, weapons and goods taken during the transition. These dates should remain separate from the entry on 19 September. Occupation did not arrive as a fully understood set of rules at one instant; its demands accumulated over the following days. The threat of severe punishment made uncertainty especially dangerous. A person might need to report to an office or surrender an item without knowing whether the instruction would remain the same the next morning.[6]

Registration was more than a means of restoring ordinary administration. It made people and institutions legible to an occupying power: where someone lived, what work they had performed and what category the authorities assigned to them could determine their treatment. A workplace list could help reopen an essential service, but it could also identify people for compulsory labour or persecution. The same act of providing information could therefore carry different consequences for different residents. The administrative language of order should not conceal the coercion behind it or the unequal status built into the occupation.

Jewish residents were subjected to abuse and persecution from the first days. This chronology is essential because it prevents the later explosions in central Kiev from being treated as the origin of German antisemitic violence. The occupiers entered with policies and institutions already directed against Jews. The attacks on individuals, seizure of property and imposition of dangerous labour were part of that initial regime. The evidence establishes responsibility in German military and security institutions rather than attributing the violence to an impersonal atmosphere of wartime disorder.[2][4]

Other residents could experience uncertainty without facing the same immediate danger. Ukrainian hopes for political change, memories of Soviet repression and ordinary relief that bombardment had paused did not create a common response to the Germans. Nor did a gesture of welcome establish consent to the regime that followed. People interpreted the arrival through different experiences and incomplete information. The historian should resist converting selected spectators into the voice of the city. Occupation imposed a hierarchy of power and vulnerability even where residents had initially imagined that it might bring something else.

The earlier occupation of Poland offers a relevant precedent for the sequence of registration, dispossession and administrative change that could follow conquest, although Kiev’s institutions and local experience require their own evidence. Conquest had already shown how military possession could be followed by registration, dispossession and reorganised authority. Kiev belonged to a different campaign and a distinct local history, but the separation between battlefield success and the treatment of an occupied population remains fundamental. A city could cease to be a defended military objective while becoming the site of new forms of organised violence. The absence of sustained street fighting after the Soviet departure did not mean that its inhabitants had entered a period of security.

The battle continues beyond the city

While occupation authorities established themselves in Kiev, Soviet headquarters were still trying to locate the armies east of it. A General Staff conversation dated 19 September records an intercepted radio message from the 5th Army’s area around Pyriatyn and Krucha asking for help before contact ceased. The higher headquarters did not possess a clear picture of Kirponos, Potapov or the neighbouring commands. This is the military counterpoint to the city’s capture: the Germans could announce possession of Kiev while Soviet officers were still searching for information about forces that had left it or fought elsewhere within the pocket.[3]

The same exchange reveals that technical connection and useful communication were not identical. Calls to the 38th Army sometimes reached signals personnel who could not answer operational questions; by the time a commander or staff officer was brought to the equipment, the connection had failed. An officer sent by aircraft had not returned when the report was made. These details explain why headquarters could not simply consult a map and redirect every formation. The map itself depended on reports that were late, incomplete or missing. Even where communications equipment functioned briefly, the right person and the necessary information might not be available together.[3]

Supply efforts continued into the following day. On 20 September, the General Staff pressed the Southwestern Direction to send fuel and ammunition by air to Kirponos’s forces, particularly to Fyodor Kostenko’s 26th Army. It reported that substantial equipment could not be moved because fuel was lacking. The planned flights had not all departed, and the small number expected was judged inadequate. This was an attempt to preserve movement and fighting capacity within the pocket, not evidence of a successful air bridge. The difference between a dispatch order and a completed delivery remained decisive.[3]

The request included using combat aircraft if necessary. That instruction demonstrates the urgency but also the limitations of improvisation. An aircraft assigned to carry supplies could not perform its usual mission at the same time, and the load it could deliver still had to reach the intended troops. Fuel was especially consequential because vehicles without it could become fixed stores of weapons and equipment rather than means of escape. Abandoning those vehicles might allow some men to move, but it would reduce the material strength with which they could continue fighting after a breakout.

Outside the main pocket, Belov’s group was still fighting around Romny. A report conveyed on 20 September described the positions reached after hard fighting on the previous day and noted the arrival or concentration of additional formations. The German eastern flank therefore remained an active front while Kiev was being occupied. This continued resistance did not reverse the encirclement, but it constrained the encircling forces and required them to retain troops facing outward. The fall of the city should not be allowed to flatten these simultaneous operations into an image of universal Soviet surrender.[3]

Medical services, transport offices and supply personnel were caught in the same fragmentation as combat units. Their loss mattered because armies depended on specialized work that could not be recreated merely by collecting survivors. A driver who escaped without his vehicle, a surgeon separated from equipment or a signals operator without a functioning network could still serve again, but the immediate organisation had been damaged. The Soviet defeat therefore involved more than the number of riflemen removed from the line. It broke relationships between people, matériel and institutions that had made large-scale resistance possible.

The General Staff responded to the information crisis by sending liaison officers as well as demanding reports. On 20 September it announced that Captain Reznik and Senior Lieutenant Saltykov were flying from Moscow to Kharkov for assignment to the 38th Army. Theatre headquarters was told to meet them, provide a map, explain the situation and send them onward by car. Their mission was to remain with the army and report by whatever means were available. This was a concrete attempt to reconnect levels of command after ordinary channels had proved insufficient. It also required scarce aircraft and vehicles for the movement of two officers whose principal resource was their ability to carry reliable information.[3]

Theatre staff protested that their available communication lines could not carry every requested form of report while replacing the functions of the missing front headquarters. Encryption introduced further delay. The exchange exposes an administrative limit to military control: demanding more information could overload the system needed to transmit it. As Kiev entered occupation, Soviet command was still trying to determine which reports were essential and how to obtain them in time to influence the fighting.[3]

Destruction after the entry

The explosions that devastated central Kiev began on 24 September, five days after the German entry. Buildings used by the occupiers had been mined by Soviet personnel, and the blasts and fires killed residents as well as Germans. Their occurrence must be distinguished from demolitions during the withdrawal and from the later German decisions directed against the Jewish population. Combining all three into one event obscures both chronology and responsibility. The demolition order of 17 September establishes an official policy of denying military resources; it does not by itself identify every device placed in the city or every person responsible for a later explosion.[3][2]

Pavliuk’s entry of 26 September records reports of the explosion two days earlier and the spread of fire through central districts. He noted uncertainty about exactly where the initial blast had occurred. That qualification matters: inhabitants were hearing, seeing and interpreting destruction while rumours moved through the city. The interruption of water service made fire an especially immediate danger. A household that had survived the transition of 18–19 September could lose its shelter during the following week. Occupation did not replace one crisis with a stable new order; it added new rules and threats while the physical conditions of urban life continued to deteriorate.[8]

The Germans blamed Jews collectively for the Soviet demolitions. That accusation was a justification chosen by the perpetrators, not an evidentiary finding. The chronology of persecution already underway before 24 September makes the point clear. The full account of the subsequent mass murder belongs to Victory and Catastrophe. Here the necessary conclusion is narrower: the first occupation days established institutions, classifications and coercive practices that exposed particular residents to danger, while the later explosions furnished those institutions with a public pretext for further violence.[2]

Responsibility for destroying infrastructure and responsibility for murdering civilians are distinct questions. Identifying Soviet demolition work does not transfer responsibility for German crimes to the people targeted by them. Identifying German persecution does not erase the suffering caused to residents by the destruction of water, power or shelter during the Soviet withdrawal. An evidence-led account can address both without treating them as equivalent policies or using one to excuse the other. The city’s inhabitants experienced consequences from decisions made by several institutions, but those institutions retained responsibility for their own actions.

What the capture accomplished

Kiev’s fall removed a major defended position from the German army’s immediate front and gave the occupiers control of an important city. It did not restore the bridges, eliminate Soviet resistance throughout the pocket or provide a functioning urban economy ready to serve German needs. The victory therefore created tasks as well as opportunities: engineers, guards, administrative staffs and transport services had to operate in a damaged environment while the armies continued fighting. German military success and the city’s civilian crisis were connected through the use of the same roads, buildings, labour and supplies.

For the Soviet command, leaving Kiev was necessary to any attempt at escape, but the authorization came after the larger routes had been cut. For residents, the army’s departure meant that their survival would depend increasingly on household resources, neighbours and decisions made by the occupying authorities. These were different forms of loss. The next chapter, The Destruction of the Pocket, follows the soldiers whose struggle continued beyond the city. Kiev remained behind them, inhabited, damaged and subject to a regime whose violence was already beginning.

Contemporary orders establish intentions, while reports contain the information, estimates and gaps known to their authors. Retrospective military accounts and testimony are identified and assessed alongside documentary evidence and scholarship. English paraphrases of Russian, Ukrainian and German texts are by the atlas unless a published translator is named. Archival references reproduced in published sources do not imply direct archival inspection. Events after the chapter date are dated explicitly. The companion map is a dated regional military reconstruction; its feature sources and precision notes distinguish reported positions from approximate connecting edges.
